planting.note: Site in full sun in well-drained soil where its tight, flattened bun shape can be appreciated up close, such as trough gardens, rock gardens, or the front of a mixed conifer bed.

directions: One of the most diminutive Norway spruce cultivars in cultivation, Little Gem forms an exceptionally flat, tight bun, adding well under an inch a year and reaching only about 8 to 10 inches tall by 18 to 20 inches wide after a decade. The short, dark green needles are densely packed on congested branching, giving the mound a fine, uniform texture without any of the pruning that flat-topped conifers of this size sometimes need. Its true-miniature scale makes it a staple of trough and rock gardens as well as miniature conifer collections, where larger bird's-nest-type spruces would quickly overwhelm the space. Give it well-drained soil and full sun; it resents standing water more than most dwarf spruces of its size.

planting.note: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; the irregular, bumpy mound form looks best as a standalone accent rather than crowded among other shrubs.

directions: One of the older German dwarf Norway spruce selections, Pusch builds a dense, irregularly bumpy mound rather than the smooth dome or nest-like depression seen in cultivars like 'Nidiformis', with short branches that pile up unevenly to give the plant a rugged, textured profile. Growth is slow, on the order of two to three inches a year, so a specimen typically holds to roughly two feet tall and three feet wide after ten years without shearing. Dark green needles stay dense to the interior of the plant, so it never develops the bare, leggy look some older dwarf spruces get with age. It is a good choice where a bird's-nest-type spruce is wanted but a less formal, more sculptural outline is preferred.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil with good air circulation; like other dwarf Alberta-type spruces it is prone to spider mites in hot, dry, still conditions.

directions: This cultivar keeps the same tight, conical silhouette as the classic dwarf Alberta spruce but replaces the straight needles with ones that curl and twist along the stem, giving the whole plant a soft, curly texture that is immediately distinguishable from 'Conica' at a glance. Growth is extremely slow and dense, building a narrow cone perhaps two to three feet tall after a decade, useful anywhere a small, formal accent is wanted without the bulk of the species. Like other Alberta-derived selections it can suffer spider mite damage and sunscald in hot, exposed, dry sites, so afternoon shade in warmer parts of its range and occasional syringing in dry weather help keep it looking its best. It is a favorite for container specimens and miniature conifer gardens.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; blue needle color develops best with full sun exposure and the flattened globe habit needs no shearing to maintain.

directions: Globosa brings the steel-blue needle color of Colorado spruce into a dwarf, wider-than-tall mounded form, growing three to five inches a year when young and settling into a broad, somewhat flat-topped globe roughly three feet tall by four to five feet wide over ten years — considerably larger at maturity than true miniature spruce cultivars, but still a fraction of the size of the 60-plus-foot species. Stiff, sharply pointed needles hold their blue-white color through the season better than many blue spruce cultivars grown from seed, since it is propagated by grafting onto stable, color-true stock. Its dense branching and broad silhouette make it a strong anchor specimen in a conifer bed or foundation planting where a smaller, rounder counterpart to the species' narrow spire form is wanted.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; left unstaked it trails as a groundcover, or stake a central leader to train a small weeping specimen tree.

directions: An Iseli Nursery introduction selected as a low, spreading sport of deodar cedar, Feelin' Blue carries the species' soft, silvery-blue needles on cascading branches that hug the ground if left unstaked, making a striking groundcover or a dramatic weeping accent draped over a wall when trained up a stake in its early years. It spreads considerably faster than it climbs, typically reaching only a foot or two tall while extending six to twelve feet wide over a decade if given the room. Like the species it wants excellent drainage and full sun and is best suited to the milder winters of zones 6 through 9, where deodar cedar is a familiar landscape conifer. Its blue color and cascading texture pair well with golden or green groundcover conifers for contrast.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; strongest gold color develops in full sun, and the low, spreading habit works well cascading over a wall or bank.

directions: Golden Horizon is Iseli Nursery's golden-foliage counterpart to their low, spreading deodar cedar selections, holding bright yellow-gold new growth that mellows to a warm gold-green with age on gracefully weeping, ground-hugging branches. Left untrained it forms a broad, low mound or cascade well suited to draping over walls and slopes; staked while young it can instead be trained into a small weeping specimen with a distinct leader. Growth is moderate for a deodar cedar but the plant stays low and wide, typically reaching just a few feet tall while spreading considerably further given the space. As with other deodar cedar selections it needs full sun for its best color and excellent drainage, and performs best in the milder winter climates of zones 6 through 9.

planting.note: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; the rounded, no-leader form needs no shearing to hold its shape.

directions: Blue Shag is a globose, leaderless selection of eastern white pine developed by American pine breeder Joel Spingarn, building a dense, rounded mound of the species' characteristically soft, blue-green needles in bundles of five. Without a dominant central leader it grows outward as much as upward, reaching roughly three feet tall by three to four feet wide after a decade, considerably more compact than seedling-grown dwarf white pines that still push a leader skyward. Its fine, shaggy texture and soft blue cast make it a favorite foreground plant in conifer collections and mixed borders where the coarser look of mugo or Austrian pine selections would feel out of place. It tolerates average garden soil but, like the species, is intolerant of wet feet and heavy clay.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; dense, irregular branching makes it a popular subject for bonsai training as well as rock garden and border use.

directions: Negishi is one of the most widely grown dwarf selections of Japanese white pine, building a dense, irregularly broad bush of short, twisted, blue-green needles banded with white stomatal lines that give the foliage a frosted, silvery cast. Growth is slow and congested from the start, producing multiple short shoots rather than a single dominant leader, so the plant develops character and irregularity early — a trait that has made it a long-standing favorite for bonsai as well as for rock gardens and border plantings. After a decade it typically reaches three to four feet in both height and width, eventually forming a picturesque small tree with age if left untrained. It prefers well-drained soil and, like other Japanese white pines, resents heavy, wet clay.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained, average soil; among the slowest-growing mugo pine selections, it needs no shearing or candle-pinching to stay compact.

directions: Selected for a growth rate even slower than most true-dwarf mugo pines, Slowmound forms a tight, symmetrical globe of dark green needles that adds well under an inch of new growth a year, reaching only about a foot tall and wide after a decade — small enough to be a mainstay of miniature conifer collections and trough gardens rather than needing the candle-pinching many mugo selections require to stay in bounds. Its dense, even branching gives the mound a neat, formal outline from the nursery pot onward. It shares the species' tolerance for poor, rocky, or alkaline soil and full sun exposure, and is a reliable, low-maintenance choice for rock gardens, entry plantings, and containers where a larger mugo cultivar would quickly outgrow the space.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; slow, dense growth and striking blue-grey needles make it a strong specimen or focal-point conifer.

directions: One of the oldest named Scots pine selections still widely grown, Watereri forms a dense, rounded-to-conical bush of short, strongly twisted, blue-grey needles that give the whole plant a silvery cast distinct from the yellow-green of the species. Growth is slow and compact compared to seedling Scots pine, typically reaching four to six feet after a decade, though given enough time it will eventually develop into a small, picturesque, flat-topped tree with the orange, plated bark the species is known for. Its congested branching and blue color have made it a long-standing favorite specimen conifer in British and American gardens alike, equally at home as a focal point in a large rock garden or as an anchor in a mixed conifer border. It tolerates poor, sandy, or rocky soil and needs excellent drainage.

planting.note: Plant in full sun to light shade in cool, moist, well-drained soil; performs best in climates with cool summers and struggles with prolonged heat.

directions: One of the classic dwarf conifer selections of balsam fir, 'Nana' forms a dense, flat-topped cushion of short, dark green needles that release the species' familiar resinous fragrance when brushed. Growth is slow, typically two inches or less a year, building a tidy mound roughly a foot to two feet tall and two to three feet wide after a decade, with a slightly depressed or irregular crown similar in spirit to bird's-nest spruce. It has long been a staple of rock gardens and miniature conifer collections in the cooler parts of its range, but performs poorly in hot, humid summer climates where balsam fir in general struggles, making it best suited to the northern tier of its hardiness range. Give it cool, consistently moist, well-drained soil and some afternoon shade where summers run hot.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; avoid humid, poorly ventilated sites, since this cultivar is prone to fungal blight in hot, sticky summers.

directions: Nicknamed the Noah's Ark juniper for its use in miniature and fairy-garden plantings, Compressa is one of the true miniature conifers, forming an exceptionally narrow, densely packed spire of blue-green needles that adds only about an inch of height a year. After a decade a well-grown specimen is typically only a foot or two tall and just a few inches wide, small enough to grow for years in a trough or alpine bed alongside true alpine perennials. Foliage takes on a bronzy cast in winter cold before greening back up in spring. It wants full sun, sharp drainage, and good air movement — this selection is notably more susceptible than the species to Phomopsis and Kabatina blight in hot, humid, still conditions, so siting and spacing for airflow matter more than with most dwarf conifers.

planting.note: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; the dense, congested habit needs no pruning to maintain its rounded shape.

directions: Tenzan is a compact, congested dwarf selection of Japanese cedar, building a dense, irregularly globose mound of short, tightly curled, blue-green needles on stubby, closely packed branchlets. It is slower and considerably smaller at a given age than well-known dwarf selections like 'Globosa Nana', typically reaching only around two feet tall and wide after ten years, with a rougher, more textured surface than that cultivar's smoother dome. Foliage picks up bronze-purple tones in cold weather, returning to blue-green with the arrival of spring growth. Its small scale and dense habit make it well suited to rock gardens and container culture as well as mixed conifer beds, and like other Japanese cedar selections it wants consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and appreciates some afternoon shade in hot climates.
